source.version: Journal version of record: Dirasat: Educational Sciences, Volume 53, No. 3, 2026, article 13368; received 28/9/2025, revised 11/12/2025, accepted 2/2/2026, published 25/2/2026 (p. 1). Body text is in Arabic; title and abstract also in English.
source.title_on_document: Effectiveness of a Training Program Based on Artificial Intelligence Tools in Developing Creative Problem-Solving Skills

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. All statistics are in Tables 1 to 7 and Figures 1 to 3 of the main text.

paper_design_summary: Seventy-five tenth-grade students in three intact mixed-gender classes of one school (Arab schools of Haifa District) were assigned by class, at random, to a 20-session creative problem-solving training program delivered with AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot), the same Osborn-Parnes program delivered with classroom strategies and no AI, or a no-training control, 25 students per class. All students took the verbal Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (form A, Jordanian adaptation) before, right after, and about three months after the program, scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality. The paper analyzes the scores with a two-way repeated-measures MANOVA and Bonferroni comparisons across measurement times.

studies.label: Classroom experiment: AI-tool training vs classroom training vs control, tenth graders, TTCT verbal

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each of three intact classes was assigned at random to one of three conditions: AI-tool-based training (second experimental group), classroom-based training (first experimental group), or control. Individual students were not reassigned across classes, so there is one class per arm.
assignment.quote: The classes were randomly assigned to three groups: the first experimental group (classroom-based training), the second experimental group (training using artificial intelligence tools), and a control group, with 25 students in each group.
assignment.locator: p. 1, English abstract (Methods); p. 6, section 'Study population and sample' (classes distributed at random under the quasi-experimental design); p. 5, section 'Limits of the study' (random assignment at the level of the research groups, with no redistribution of individuals within classes); p. 9, design diagram (R for each group)

arms.name: AI-tool training (second experimental group, 2EG)
arms.description: 20-session creative problem-solving program based on the Osborn-Parnes model (objective, fact, problem, idea, solution, and acceptance finding), with training activities using ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in the computer lab. 3 sessions per week, 45 minutes each (opening and closing sessions 60 minutes), 4 May to 12 June 2025.

arms.name: Classroom training (first experimental group, 1EG)
arms.description: The same Osborn-Parnes training program delivered inside the classroom without AI tools, using brainstorming, problem-based learning, project-based learning, think-pair-share, flipped learning, and synectics.

arms.name: Control (CG)
arms.description: No training program. Took the same pre-, post-, and follow-up tests.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The paper states 25 students per group at assignment; no table prints the analyzed n, but the error degrees of freedom of 72 in the MANOVA (Table 5, p. 11) match 75 students in three groups. Per-arm analyzed counts of 25 assume no attrition, which the paper does not state explicitly.
participants.who: Tenth-grade students (41 boys, 34 girls), three intact mixed-gender classes in one school, selected by convenience because of the first author's workplace. Study population: 3,719 tenth graders in 38 Arab schools of Haifa District.
participants.country: Arab schools of Haifa District 'inside the Green Line' (Israel), as the paper describes the setting; authors at Yarmouk University, Jordan
participants.quote: The sample comprised 75 students distributed across three intact mixed-gender tenth-grade classes in a single school.
participants.locator: p. 1, English abstract (Methods); p. 6, section 'Study population and sample'

ai_tool.how_used: Students in the AI arm used the three chatbots in structured training sessions in the computer lab, one tool per session (Table 2): ChatGPT for interactive dialogue and generating many ideas (fluency), Gemini for varied ideas across contexts (flexibility), Copilot for new and unusual solutions (originality). The tests themselves were taken in the opening and closing sessions (no AI tool listed for those sessions) and at a follow-up.

task.description: Verbal Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, form A, in the Jordanian adaptation by Al-Shanti (1983): six verbal subtests (the sixth of seven dropped), scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality. The paper defines creative problem solving operationally as the TTCT scores.
task.duration: Test duration not stated. Training: 20 sessions, 3 per week, 45 minutes each (opening and closing 60 minutes), 4 May to 12 June 2025.

outcomes.name: TTCT fluency, post-test
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: TTCT verbal fluency score (number of responses), hand-scored. Scoring reliability: agreement between two scorers 0.75 (Holsti formula); test-retest 0.80 on a 25-student pilot sample (Table 1, p. 6).
outcomes.delay: Post-test given in the final (20th) session, which lists no AI tool (Table 2, p. 9; Procedures, p. 10).

contrasts.reported: Post-test mean (SD): AI training 41.32 (8.01) vs classroom training 33.56 (11.24); pre-test 24.64 (7.30) vs 22.80 (13.02); n = 25 per group. Omnibus 3-group tests over pre, post, follow-up: group x test interaction F = 25.328, p = 0.000, partial eta squared 0.413; group main effect F = 17.065, p = 0.000, eta squared 0.322 (error df 72). No pairwise between-group test is printed.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear: three intact classes were randomly assigned to three conditions (p. 1; p. 5, Limits; p. 6), so assignment is random only at the class level, with one class per arm; the paper itself calls the design quasi-experimental, and the AI arm also bundles the training program (versus the no-training control). Criterion 2 is met: 75 students, 25 per arm, and the MANOVA error df of 72 imply 75 analyzed (Table 5, p. 11). Criterion 3 is met: TTCT verbal fluency, flexibility, and originality scored on the students' test responses, taken after the AI training ended (an after_ai outcome).

one_line_finding: After 20 AI-tool training sessions, the AI class scored highest on the verbal TTCT post-test (fluency 41.32 vs 33.56 classroom training vs 21.68 control; flexibility 29.04 vs 24.88 vs 16.48; originality 29.32 vs 19.48 vs 8.51; Table 4, pp. 10-11), with significant group x time interactions (eta squared 0.41 to 0.59; Table 5, p. 11) and no significant decline at follow-up (Tables 6-7, p. 12).
open_questions: Does random assignment of three intact classes, one per arm, satisfy criterion 1? With one cluster per arm, class and condition are confounded, and the MANOVA treats students as independent units.

The paper does not state explicitly that AI was unavailable during the TTCT. The post-test was given in the closing session, for which Table 2 lists no AI tool, and the control class took the same test, so the outcome is coded after_ai with AI not available.
Is the AI-training vs classroom-training contrast best coded ai_vs_active? Both arms received the same Osborn-Parnes program; only the delivery (AI tools vs classroom strategies) differed.

No pairwise between-group test is printed; Tables 6 and 7 compare measurement times within each group. Between-arm statistics are means, SDs, and n = 25 per arm, plus omnibus 3-group F tests that pool pre-, post-, and follow-up scores.
Pre-test fluency differed across classes (AI 24.64, classroom 22.80, control 20.40); the paper reports no baseline equivalence test.
notes: The body text is Arabic, and the markdown conversion scrambles the right-to-left text, so all entries were read from the PDF page images. Table 4 rows labelled 'total' are grand means across the three groups, not a total creativity score, so no overall_creativity outcome is listed. Table 3 (p. 10) reports Mauchly's test; Huynh-Feldt corrections were applied. Assumption checks: Kolmogorov-Smirnov 0.083, 0.084, 0.078; Box's M 1.342 (p. 10). The program sessions ran within general culture and activity periods (p. 10), so the setting is ordinary schooling; coded field_rct with class as the unit of assignment.
